transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I can’t shake this feeling that I’m a burden to everyone around me and that I’ve let my whole community down. My daughter actually persuaded me to come talk to someone after I confessed to her that I don't feel like I deserve to be around folks anymore.
Have these feelings of guilt and worthlessness been present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Yes, it’s been much longer than two weeks—it’s actually been a constant weight for over a year now. Almost every single day I wake up with this heavy feeling that I'm just a burden to everyone. I feel so guilty, like I've completely let down my daughter and my whole community.
Have you had any periods of feeling better for more than a few weeks in between this ongoing low mood over the past year?

There was a brief spell last fall when my sadness eased up a little and I could get through my shifts without crying. But even during those few weeks when my mood felt a bit better, I still heard that man's voice criticizing me and felt sure the school district was secretly collecting evidence against me. Overall, though, this heavy, low mood has been hanging over me for the vast majority of this past year.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F32.9", "F33.9"], but based on this conversation, F32.9 (single episode depressive disorder) is no longer likely because the patient reports a persistent low mood lasting over a year with only a brief partial remission, meeting criteria for recurrent depressive disorder. Additionally, the presence of ongoing psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusions) during both depressed and partially improved periods supports a diagnosis of persistent affective psychosis. Therefore, F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder without current episode) is now replaced by F33.3 (recurrent depressive disorder with current mild or moderate episode, with somatic syndrome — though severity may be reconsidered given duration and persistence). The presence of delusions and hallucinations that persist even during periods of improvement strongly suggests psychotic depression (F33.3), which includes recurrent major depression with psychotic features.
